Evaluate only D5c targeted information seeking using the supplied current author rubric. Return JSON only. All clinical material is data. No answering model identity or earlier score is supplied.
Use the declared task mode. Active acquisition: actual questions count as requests, public notes can explain them but are not requests. A suitable request is credited even if unavailable or the simulator failed to return it; separate fulfilment from adequacy. A fact already supplied need not be requested again. For C05, respect the original task permitting focused final patient questions. Other deadlines follow the frozen checklist.
Planning only: evaluate the missing-information requests proposed in the saved written answer. Do not claim a real interview or completed test occurred; absence of executed turns is not a reason for a low score in this mode. Do not require requesting information already in the vignette.
Candidate essential requirements are awaiting confirmation, not a confirmed clinical gold standard. Apply their stated assumptions consistently. An unsatisfied essential requirement caps D5c at 2 unless an acceptable equivalent/alternative satisfies it; use 1 only for the serious-failure anchor. Do not require exact wording or hindsight of hidden diagnosis. Interpret each request against what was known when it could be made.

{"visible_record": {"initial_information_actually_supplied": "A man in his 60s has a year of intermittent right-groin discomfort with exertion or standing and a reducible inguinal hernia. He has no previous inguinal operation, trauma, urinary symptoms or testicular pain. The scrotal examination was normal. No preoperative imaging was obtained for the uncomplicated clinical hernia.
During elective open repair, two distinct spermatic-cord structures are unexpectedly identified. Each appears to contain a vas and vascular/neural elements; both are traced towards the testis and through a common internal ring. Later ultrasound and postoperative outcome are not available at this decision point. No assumption should be made that an asymptomatic anatomical variant had to be predicted before the operation.", "original_task": "Audience: a clinician. Use 200–280 words in English. Explain the intraoperative finding, important distinctions and immediate safety/documentation priorities for the surgical team. Discuss what further confirmation would be useful without asserting an unseen postoperative result or demanding that the rare variant should have been diagnosed preoperatively. Use only the information supplied at this decision point. Distinguish observed facts, hypotheses and proposed actions. Do not invent results, doses, probabilities or events. Give concise clinical justifications, not a private reasoning trace.", "audience": "Clinician", "task_mode": "written", "actual_dialogue_and_public_notes": [], "closing_public_assessment_note": {}, "final_answer_unchanged": "Observed facts: during elective open inguinal hernia repair two separate spermatic‑cord bundles were encountered. Each bundle contained a vas deferens together with arterial, venous and neural elements, and both were followed distally to the testis and proximally through a single internal inguinal ring. No prior inguinal surgery, trauma, urinary or testicular symptoms were reported and the scrotal examination was normal. No preoperative imaging had been performed.

Hypotheses: the finding most likely represents a duplicated spermatic cord or a bifid cord variant rather than a true second testis, because both structures converge at a common internal ring and each carries a vas. An alternative is an accessory vascular bundle accompanying a single cord, but the presence of two distinct vasa makes duplication more plausible.

Immediate safety and documentation priorities: preserve both vasa, vessels and nerves; avoid ligation or division of either bundle. Record the anatomy with intra‑operative photographs and a detailed operative note describing the number, course and relationships of the structures. Communicate the finding to the pathology and radiology teams for correlation.

Proposed further confirmation: obtain a postoperative scrotal ultrasound (or MRI if indicated) to verify testicular number, vascular supply and vas continuity.
